newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Clarke says cabinet united on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Clarke says cabinet united on EMU.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday said the government was in accord on European monetary union and blamed the press for twisting his words into a fresh divide within the ruling party.
In an interview at the weekend, Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said it would be "pathetic" for Britain to wait and see how a single European currency developed before deciding whether to join.
The comments immediately sparked fury within his party and an attack from right-winger Nicholas Bonsor, a junior foreign office minister, who accused him of being out of line with government policy.

"I've said nothing at the weekend that I haven't said countless times before," Clarke told reporters in this Caribbean island where he arrived on Tuesday for a Commonwealth finance ministers' meeting.
In his first publc comments since the row erupted, Clarke said he and Prime Minister John Major were in complete accord on the issue.

"It seems to me the whole thing is a fuss about nothing. No one who listened to the radio interview could have recognised it as the reporting that appeared in the British press," he said as he entered the hotel where he was due to address some 30 Commonwealth finance ministers.
"The whole thing has been a fabrication."

His comments at the weekend were seen as a fresh split within the Conservative party, whose vocal right-wing wants Major to bar entry into a single currency with other members of the European Union for the life of the next five-year parliament.

Commenting on calls for his resignation, Clarke, seen as a supporter of a single currency, said it would be foolish to quit simply for repeating the government line on the issue which the cabinet agreed on in April.
"Go and ask Sir Nicholas Bonsor...I certainly wouldn't rely on your description of what Sir Nicholas Bonsor said," Clarke retorted when asked for a reaction to Bonsor's comments.
Major's office has issued denials of any rift on the issue.

Senior pro-Europeans in the past few days have gone on the offensive in public to counter the so-called Eurosceptics in the party whom they fear are dominating the political debate in the run-up to the next general election within eight months.

The opposition Labour Party is far ahead in opinion polls and Conservative strategists worry that the European debate will take over their party conference -- the last before an election -- in October.
